title: Inheritance
body:
One of the four OO pillars. A subclass takes on the attributes and operations of its
superclass and adds or overrides what makes it different, so the shared part is written once.
`Savings account **is a** bank account.` The relationship is *is-a*, and that phrase is the
test.

What the course claims it buys: **extensibility**. Adding a new kind of account means adding
a subclass, not editing the existing ones, and the code that works in terms of the base class
keeps working. That only pays off in combination with [[Polymorphism]], which is what lets
existing code call the new subclass without knowing it exists. Inheritance without
polymorphism is just shared fields.

## Where it goes wrong

Inheritance is the most over-used of the four pillars, because it is the easiest way to share
code and sharing code is not what it is for.

- **Not-really-is-a.** If `Stack` inherits from `ArrayList` to get the storage, every
  `ArrayList` operation is now on the stack's [[Interface]], including the ones that break
  it. The relationship was *has-a*. Use composition: hold the list as a field.
- **It is the tightest coupling there is.** A subclass depends on its parent's internals, not
  just its interface, so a change to the parent can break every subclass silently. See
  [[Coupling and Cohesion]].
- **Deep hierarchies.** Once a tree is five levels deep, understanding one class means
  reading five, and "where is this method actually defined" stops being answerable by eye.
  Depth of inheritance is a standard [[Metrics|metric]] for this.

Modern practice is to prefer composition and reserve inheritance for genuine *is-a* with a
stable base class.

See also [[Classes]], [[Object]], [[OOD]], and [[Java]], where `extends` is the keyword and
single inheritance is enforced (interfaces are how Java gets the multiple-parent case without
the ambiguity).
